en: Śrīḥ!
An Investigation into the Function of Words, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Mammaṭācārya.
In this context, the rejection of what is to be abandoned and the acceptance of what is to be adopted arise solely from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that [cognition] possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge by virtue of its nature as a definitive ascertainment (*niścaya*). Furthermore, such ascertainment takes the object as its domain in conjunction with the word.
Since a word functions as an instrument because its causal activity— the cognition of the object— is otherwise inexplicable,

the operation (vyāpāra) postulated for it— conveyed by terms such as "denotation" (abhidhā) and so forth— is manifold; therefore, this treatise, consisting of an investigation into the operation of words, is commenced for the purpose of examining that [manifold nature].
And since it is not appropriate to demonstrate the operation by pointing to each individual case, it is shown by way of its objects:
"The denoted meaning consists of genus, action, quality, or name; the sound is combined with these."
Since there is no comprehension of meaning from a word for which a convention has not been grasped, a word conveys its meaning only with the assistance of convention.
Therefore, "samita" means that sound or word which has been conventionally established (*saṅketita*) with respect to a certain object;
it is so called because that object was previously perceived [in association with it], and not otherwise.
The "primary" (mukhya) is the expressed meaning (vācya), the denoted object (abhidheya-artha), which is well-known as the locus of rest. Thus he says: "the genus," and so forth.
Although in this context the individual (vyakti) alone is the actual object of engagement and withdrawal, [it is nevertheless designated by the term "genus"].

Nevertheless, because [the individual] is infinite and because of deviation, it is impossible to establish a convention for it; furthermore, so that the words "cow," "white," "moving," and "Dittha" do not result in having a single referent, the convention for words is established only with respect to an attribute (*upādhi*).

An adjunct (*upādhi*) is both a property of a real entity and one imposed by the whim of the speaker. The former is twofold: established (*siddha*) and to be established (*sādhya*). The established [adjunct] is also of two kinds: that which bestows life upon the category of the object (*padārtha*), and the cause for the addition of specific qualities (*viśeṣādhāna-hetu*).
And: the first [of these] is the genus (*jāti*).
For it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "A cow is neither a cow by its own nature, nor is it a non-cow; rather, it is a cow through its connection with cowness (*gotva*)."
This is the second quality:

for an object whose existence has been established by means of [qualities] such as whiteness is thereby qualified. That which is to be accomplished (sādhya) consists of parts occurring in a temporal sequence and has the nature of action (kriyā).

The nature of words such as "Ḍittha" and others— which is grasped by the final cognition and in which the sequence [of phonemes] has been withdrawn— is established by the speaker at will as an adjunct upon objects such as the person named Ḍittha;
thus, it is said that the form of a name consists of arbitrariness (*yadṛcchā*).
In the Bhāṣya, a fourfold application of words is stated regarding such instances as "cow," "white," "moving," and "Ḍittha";
however, since qualities such as *paramāṇutva* (atomicity) are included among the list of qualities (*guṇa*), their status as a quality is technical (*pāribhāṣika*).

Now, one might object: in the case of qualities such as whiteness residing in substrates like milk or a conch shell, that universal which exists by virtue of which the designation and cognition "white, white" occur without distinction is "whiteness-ness" (*śuklatva*) and so forth;
likewise, in the cooking of molasses, rice, and the like, there is similarly [the universal] "cooking-ness" (*pākatva*) and so on.

Furthermore, in the case of sounds uttered by parrots, mainas, and the like, such as the word "Ḍittha," and in the case of the referents "Ḍittha" and so on—wherein the nature of the word "Ḍittha" changes at every moment—how could there be a fourfold application of words if the "Ḍittha-ness" did not exist in the referent "Ḍittha"? It is said in reply:
although there is a difference among individuals due to their shape, configuration, size, and color, [the universal] "cow" exists in a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and a white cow (*dhāvaleya*).

Thus, the status of being the cause of a single cognition belongs to the universal (*jāti*) alone; for even though there is a difference between the *haṃsa* and the *hāra*, between clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and molasses (*guḍa*), between the words "ḍittha" and so forth uttered by parrots, mainas, and others, and between the various objects denoted as "ḍittha" and so forth, [the cognition remains the same]: "The *haṃsa* is white,"...
The necklace is white;
ghee is being cooked;
molasses is being cooked.
The word "Ḍittha" is the word "Ḍittha";

because it is the basis for the cognition of a single form—namely, "Ḍittha, Ḍittha"—qualities, actions, and proper names possess only a single form. Therefore, these are not the cause of a non-differentiated designation and cognition with respect to distinct objects.
Since "birth" (jāti) is applicable, there are exactly four grounds for the application of words.
Another says:
"When that [word] is sublated, either by conventional usage (rūḍhi) or by the sense (artha), that which is connected with it must be indicated (lakṣaṇīya). (1)

In cases such as "one skilled in words" (*śabde kuśalaḥ*), there is a sublation of the primary meaning because the grasping of *darbha* grass and so forth is impossible; and in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), there is a sublation of the primary meaning because it is impossible for the Gaṅgā and such to be the locus of a hamlet. This occurs due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—that is, established common knowledge—and likewise [due to the impossibility of the primary sense], as in "the bank of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgātaṭa*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ityādeḥ," for those who do not have such an understanding, there is a purpose consisting in the communication of [qualities] such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*) in that manner.
Thus, the indicated meaning (*lakṣaṇīya*), which is the object of the operation of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), is connected with that primary meaning (*mukhyo 'rthaḥ*).
And the connection (*saṃbandha*) here is [the quality of] distinctness (*vivekatva*) and so forth.
And there is proximity and so forth.
Thus, the two operations based on the meanings of the signified and the signifier are denotation (*abhidhā*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
[These are characterized by] the projection of another for one's own establishment, and the surrendering of oneself for the sake of another.
It is said that this purity itself is twofold: as grasping and as characteristic. // 2 //

In expressions such as "bring in the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*) or "bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), persons who are in contact with the spears and so forth are implied by means of the spears themselves for the sake of accomplishing their own entry;
therefore, this is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of the material cause (*upādāna*).

In such cases as "A cow is to be bound," the individual is implied by the genus so that the binding enjoined by the Veda may be accomplished for [the speaker], but it is not denoted by the word itself.

According to the maxim, "The denotative power, being exhausted in the qualifier, cannot reach the qualified," the *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* (indicative function based on inclusion) should not be cited here. No.
In this case, there is either a purpose or a conventional usage;
however, because of the inseparable connection with the individual, the universal implies the individual, just as in the command "let it be done," the agent is implied.
In the case of "Do it," the object (*karman*) is [the action];

in "Enter the ball" and so forth, [the objects] are "the house" and "eat" respectively. Furthermore, in the statement "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," eating at night is not indicated by indication (*lakṣyate*).
Because that [implied object] is the object of either presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) or presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*);
as in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges," where the bank is the locus of the hamlet.
In such cases as "the word *gaṅgā* conveys its own primary meaning for the sake of [conveying] perfection (*siddhi*)," this is indication by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā-lakṣaṇā*).
And this [indication] is of two kinds; it is pure (*śuddhā*) because it is unmixed with metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*).
In these two types [of indication], neither the indicated (lakṣya) nor the indicator (lakṣaka) possesses a state of external neutrality (taṭasthatva) in the form of a difference;
for when banks and so forth are conveyed by words such as "Ganges," it is only upon the comprehension of that identity (tattva) that the intended purpose is fully realized.

But if there were only the cognition of a mere connection with the Gaṅgā, what would be the difference between this and the primary verbal expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgātaṭe ghoṣaḥ), which constitutes indication (lakṣaṇā)?
But another [type of indication] is *sāropā* (superimposition), where both the object and the subject are stated as such;

that is, where the thing being superimposed and the locus of superimposition are indicated in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with their difference unmasked, that is *sāropā* indication.
When another [object] is included within the subject, that [metaphor] would be *sādhyavasānikā* (one with a determined object). // 3 //

When the object of superimposition (the *āropya*) has internalized— that is, swallowed up— the other, which is the actual locus of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*), it is *sādhyavasānā* (metaphorical identification).
These two types [of *rūpaka*] are to be understood as being either "qualified" (*gauṇa*) or "pure" (*śuddha*), depending on whether they arise from similarity or from another relationship.
These two, consisting of superimposition (*āropa*) and determination (*adhyavasāna*), are caused by similarity, as in the cases "the Vāhīka is a cow" and "this is a cow.

Regarding this, some maintain that the qualities such as dullness and sluggishness, which accompany the primary meaning (*svārtha*) and are themselves being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*), serve as the cause for the word "cow" to denote the secondary meaning (*parārtha*).

Others maintain that, through the non-difference from the qualities associated with its own meaning, it is only the qualities residing in the meaning of another that are indicated (*lakṣyante*), and not the meaning of another itself that is directly expressed (*abhidhīyate*).
This is because the meaning of another is [indicated] by resorting to qualities common [to both].
Others maintain that it is perceived in this very way;
and it has been stated elsewhere:
"Indication (lakṣaṇā) is said to be the cognition of that which is invariably connected with the primary meaning."
"Metaphorical usage (gauṇatā) is accepted as arising from the connection with qualities perceived [in the primary object].

Here, "inseparable relation" (avinābhāva) refers merely to a general connection and not to essential concomitance (nāntarīyakatva); for if it were the latter, [the metaphorical application] in cases such as "the platforms are shouting" would be impossible.
There would be no indication (lakṣaṇā).

And it has been stated that since [the meaning] is established through implication alone when there is an inseparable connection (avinābhāva), there is no utility for indication. By one who says "a dullness and sluggishness similar to the dullness and sluggishness residing in a cow," and so forth, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a universal of quality (guṇajāti) if the non-difference of qualities is admitted.

The fourfold application of words that has been stated is contradicted [in cases such as] "clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*) or "this is indeed life" (*āyur evedam*), where, due to similarity, there exists another relation— such as the relation of cause and effect— that is distinct from [the other three].
In such cases, there is first a superimposition and a subsequent determination characterized by the relation of cause and effect and so forth.
Here, although there is a distinction between the two types of secondary metaphor (*gauṇa*), the purpose is the cognition of identity and the complete apprehension of non-difference.
However, in the case of the pure and the differentiated, [properties] such as causal efficacy are established through their distinction from other things and their non-deviation;
in some instances, there is a metaphorical application based on being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), as for example:
The pillar is Indra because it exists for the sake of Indra; sometimes this is due to the relationship of property and owner, as when one says "the king's man" is the king. Sometimes...
Because of the relationship between part and whole, as in the case of "the hand's tip," where "hand" refers to the part consisting of the tip alone;
and in some cases, because of performing that function.
Just as one who is not a carpenter is called a "carpenter" [by metaphor], so too is indication (lakṣaṇā) of six kinds. // 4 //
Together with the two initial divisions,
that [suggestion] is differentiated by the differences in form among the speaker, the sentence, and the expressed meaning.
Among these, it arises from a thorough consideration of the speaker's own nature.
It goes like this:
"Much has been done for you there; what more need be said? You have displayed supreme goodness. O friend, always acting in just this way, remain happy for a hundred autumns."
This is the speech of someone who is being tormented by many injuries.
Therefore, by the power of the speaker, the word "Bṛhaspati" indicates, through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the foolishness of a fool and the villainy of a wrongdoer.
For example, from the discernment of a specific statement:
"Blessed are you, who, even during the intervals of love-making with your beloved, can utter hundreds of confident and flattering words."
And when my hand was placed upon the knot of my garment by my beloved, O friends, I swear that I remember nothing at all.
In this case, it is perceived that "I am blessed";
here, the power belongs to the sentence itself, as is seen from the determination of the specific nature of the expressed meaning— just as follows:
For you, whose power is intent on granting fearlessness to the world and who accepts all wealth offered to you,
there is no fault of ascending to an equal burden.
O wise one, no one at any time is able to do so.
In this case, one who remains indifferent even during the misfortune of a friend dear as life, and is unable to give even a blade of grass, is to be censured.
Thus, three varieties of the *dvika* (two-membered) compound and one variety of the *trika* (three-membered) compound are to be illustrated:
"O neighbor, will you cast your glance here in our house for even a moment?"
"Perhaps your father will not drink these tasteless waters from the well;
therefore, I shall go quickly from here alone to that stream thick with *tamāla* trees.
Let the joints of the reeds, with their hard-cut ends, scratch my body as they press closely together."
Thus,
having already attained glory, why would he subject me again to that labor of churning?
Nor do I even imagine that his former sleep could possibly recur for one whose mind is so free from sloth.
"Why does he build the bridge again?"— as you approach, followed by the lords of all the islands, the ocean appears as if it were harboring such doubts, and thus its trembling manifests.
Thus,
here the arrows of Love are irresistible, Mādhava unfolds in every direction,
the moonbeams cause madness in the heart, and the cuckoos captivate the mind.
O friend, how can these five unbearable fires now be endured by you, who are in another fresh stage of life and find this body difficult to sustain due to the weight of your lofty breasts?

And here, the *vastu* (the underlying fact) consists of the concealment of her enjoyment with another man by means of bringing river water, and the concealment of the nail-marks and tooth-wounds likely [inflicted] by writing with a reed-grass knot; furthermore,
there is the figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) known as *rūpaka* (metaphor), namely "you are Hari."
And since the rasa of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) is not perceived [here], it need not be cited as an example;
for there is no sublation of the primary meaning.

For it is possible for even the "innumerable" (asaṃkhyā) to be designated as "number" (saṃkhyā); furthermore, if a suggested figure were to be considered the primary object of definition (lakṣya), it would follow that when one brings fire, the act of bringing a vessel would also be the primary object of definition.
Moreover, it is only the literal meaning (vācya) that is uncontradicted which brings about the apprehension of rasa.
And when there is a purpose for indication (lakṣaṇā), an operation distinct from that [purpose] must necessarily be admitted;
and such being the case, indication occurs when there is a purpose.
And that [indication] is not to be understood from another means of valid cognition as being caused by the sublation of the primary meaning;
for it is precisely for that purpose that the term "indication" (lakṣaṇā) is employed.
Indeed, perception does not operate upon an object known through verbal testimony, nor does inference preceded by that [perception] operate thereon.
It is not another inference, because that would lead to an infinite regress;
nor is it memory, because there has been no prior experience of that [object]; or even if such memory existed, there would be no necessary recollection. Therefore...
In this case, the word itself is the means of valid cognition;
yet the word is devoid of activity and does not produce the cognition of the object,
nor is there an activity called "denotation."

In that case, because there is no conventional designation (*saṅketa*), there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for while that [indication] exists when such a designation is present, it does not have that [primary object] as its domain,
nor does it apply to the indicated object (*lakṣya*).

There is an objection: because there would be an absence of both a subject to be characterized (*lakṣya*) and a purpose (*prayojana*), as well as an absence of a relationship and a purpose [for that relationship], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding its definition as well; thus, there could be no indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And that [purpose] exists;
therefore, an operation directed toward the object of the purpose must be admitted.
And that [process] is to be designated by such verbal usages as *dhvanana* (resounding), *avagamana* (comprehension), *prakāśana* (manifestation), and *dyotana* (illumination).

Now, one might object: "The cognition of an object that does not arise from its own direct word, such as 'a hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā' (*gaṅgātaṭe ghoṣaḥ*), is exactly what is produced by expressions such as 'a hamlet on the Gaṅgā' (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*);
moreover, the bank and so forth are indicated (*lakṣyate*) as being characterized by qualities such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*). Thus, [the meaning is already] qualified."
The secondary function (lakṣaṇā) does not reside in the indicated object itself, for its specific qualities [are not directly denoted].
For if it were so, one would have to accept a fourth operation: a relationship of attribute and substrate (dharmadharmibhāva) between the riverbank and such properties as sanctity.
And how could the fruit of indication be produced by something else?
Furthermore, the operation consisting of manifestation cannot be the operation whose nature is indication.
If it is argued that this [word] is the word itself, no; for in that case, there would be no purpose for metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā),
and therefore only something qualified is indicated.
It is said:
the bank and so forth are the objects of indication (lakṣaṇā), and yet qualities such as sanctity do not exist therein.
In that case, how can there be indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to a qualified [object]?

Furthermore, since linguistic convention (saṅketa) is established based on a universal, how could that indication—by means of a distinction in convention consisting of a triad—make the qualified object its domain? It is manifested.
But it is indeed not designated by convention.
Furthermore, the object of indication (lakṣya) is the domain of indication (lakṣaṇā), not the purpose (prayojana).
For [this applies to] perception (pratyakṣa).
Blue is the object;
manifestation or consciousness is the result.
And because it is non-deviant, the cognition of the characterized object is stated to be the result.

For in this way, even regarding the result of denotation, the result of the expressive word is indeed cognition; and that [cognition] is not possible without an operation (*vyāpāra*). Nor can there be an operation of an operation; therefore, this [result] must be expressed by the word itself.

And since the result, which possesses an operation, conforms to the presence and absence of the defining characteristics [of that operation], that [operation] is its effect, and the effect is called the result;
this applies to that which is to be attained through another action.

Just as the fruit of a sacrifice is [the result], so too the fruit of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the purpose brought about by its expressive power. Just as for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is blue, the fruit is either the manifestation or the consciousness residing precisely in the blue, in the same way, for indication, [the fruit] resides in that very object.
This is the purpose.

Therefore, no other distinct operation is required to conceptualize the relationship between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin). Consequently, it is established that an operation distinct from indication (lakṣaṇā) must be resorted to.
However, another [type of indication] is established by convention (*nirūḍhā*), while yet another must be employed in a different manner.

Among words such as *anuloma* (favorable) and *pratikūla* (adverse), that [conventional indication] is established like a denotative word (*vācaka*) with respect to the indicated meaning (*lakṣya-artha*), having set aside the literal meaning. But another [type of indication] must be performed when there is sublation of the primary meaning, a cause, and a purpose.
Deprived of its splendor by the sun, its orb shrouded in frost, the moon does not shine, like a mirror blinded by breath.

In such cases as these, because words like "blind" and so forth would be inapplicable [if taken literally], the expressed meaning is completely set aside; thus, the suggested meaning is the "extraordinariness" (*asāmānyatva*) of the indicated quality of "lusterlessness. Likewise:
"That man is he, and he lives, honored..."
In this world, his fame— accumulated through valor and now sprouted anew— traverses this earth together with the rays of the sun.

In such instances, because the word *puruṣa* (man) is not [directly] applicable [to the context], its literal meaning is transferred (*saṅkramitavācya*) to suggest qualities such as valor inherent to itself, which are indicated by the word.

Just as the word *dvirepha* is employed for a "six-footed" creature (a bee) when it denotes that which is designated by words containing two *repha*s (the syllables *bha-ra*), so too the word *dvika* and others may be used for the cuckoo and so forth; otherwise, they should not be employed.
And since that [connection] was stated subsequently through positive concomitance (*anvaya*),

it is not possible here— due to infinity and because of deviation— to establish a convention for a word upon a word-meaning in its specific form, as one does for a sentence-meaning in the case of a sentence; therefore, the convention applies only to the universal (*sāmānya*).

The specific character (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of word-meanings consists in the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the general meanings already expressed, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
And thus, even that which is not itself a word-meaning becomes the sentence-meaning.
It is conveyed by the power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*).

In this view, first there is denotation (*abhidhā*), and then, when the syntactic connection is obstructed, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), it occurs first. (Verse 5)

Having observed that upon hearing the speech of an elder, such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," the middle-aged person performs a specific activity, the learner understands that the indivisible sentence is the expressive unit for the indivisible meaning.
Then, when other sentences such as "Yajñadatta, bring the cow" are employed, through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [he grasps] the restricted [meaning].

Because one determines the fixed meaning, the convention (*saṅketa*) of words applies only to a specific object delimited by the universal; thus, there is denotation (*abhidhāna*) only of things that are already related, and this constitutes the status of the word-meaning as something qualified.
In this view, prior to the act of denotation...
First, there is indication (lakṣaṇā), because it is precisely the qualified [object] that constitutes the word-meaning; thus,
both [functions] exist in both cases.
In the two-fold position— that there is *abhihitānvaya* with respect to the words and *anvitābhidhāna* with respect to the sentence— both [theories] apply;
that [function of] denotation occurs both before and after [the cognition of the relation].
In the case of an indivisible sentence-meaning, there is no reality [to individual words];
the sentence alone is the signifier of the sentence-meaning,
for just as phonemes have no meaning within words, so too do words have no meaning within sentences.
Consequently, there is no such thing as *lakṣaṇā* (indication) at all.

Just as from the utterance of the word "whip" (*kaśā*) there arises the intuition that "I have been sent by him for running," so too, through the power of intuition, comprehension arises from a qualified sentence; thus, that [intuition] alone is the meaning of the sentence.

Just as there is the conceptualization of unreal and non-existent causes, conditions, and so forth, so too, regarding the conceptualization of the referents of words within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*),
there are three positions among those already mentioned. Furthermore, they say that the basis for the ground of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is fivefold, as it has been stated:

"Indicative function (lakṣaṇā) is considered to be fivefold: through connection with the denoted meaning, through similarity, through inherence, through contrariety, and through connection with action.
In this context, for a word such as *dvirepha*, the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*) is the word "bee" (*bhramara*).
Because of that connection, the six-footed [bee] is indicated by it; this is "being based on a connection with the denoted object.
By way of similarity, as for example: "The boy is a lion," or likewise—

Throughout the entire year, this single day is uniquely praiseworthy— a day that, by its greatness, must be pursued through many days, and which neither those who came before nor those who follow can equal.
In this context, by virtue of the subject matter, a certain Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) is indicated, in whose family previous or future persons do not attain equality.
"Conjunction" (samavāya) is a relation other than the relations already mentioned. Therefore, as follows:
[The manuscript is fragmentary here:
"The hamlet is on the Ganges" by proximity;
"the umbrella-bearers are going" by association.
For in this case, even those without umbrellas are designated as such by association with those who possess umbrellas;
conversely, it is like calling a coward "Bhārgava."
Just as Pṛthu by his deeds, Rāma by his virtues, Nala by his fame, and Bharata by his majesty, so are you Śatrughna in great battle; and as Janaka is by his steadfastness, so are you.
Thus, O King, since you bear the form of ancient sovereigns through your virtuous deeds, how could you not be Māndhātṛ, even though you are a conqueror of the three worlds?
In this context, even though Aśvatthāman is not a "slayer of enemies" (śatru-ghna), he is designated as such because of his connection with the act of slaying enemies.
The suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha)—which is endowed with clarity, skill, and the like, and which possesses both denotation and indication—is renowned as *dhvani*. (6)

Just as a denotative word (*abhidhāyaka*) and an indicative word (*lakṣaka*) function through convention (*saṃketa*) together with the triad of conditions such as the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*), or just as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) accompanied by the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) leads to the inference of what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣā*), so too the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the indicated word (*lakṣyaka*)— dependent upon the knowledge of the speaker’s intention, the purity and refinement of the audience, the context, and other factors— reveal the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-artha*) through the term *dhvani*.
Among these, an example of what is suggested and revealed by the words is as follows: "O merchant, where could we get elephant tusks or tiger skins?"
...until the daughter-in-law, with her face disheveled by bees, wanders about the house.
"O merchant, where can we obtain ivory and tiger-skins,
as long as our daughter-in-law with her face framed by disheveled locks wanders about the house?
This is an example of what is revealed by the sentence (*vākya-prakāśya*).
The self sinks here; look well here for me, O traveler! Do not sink into my bed, you who are blind at night.
"Here my mother-in-law bathes; having looked here during the day,
O traveler blind at night, do not plunge into our bed!"—
here, the suggestion is rooted in the literal expression (*abhidhāna*).
An example based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) is as follows: "Like a mirror blinded by breath," which has been cited [as an example].
That same [indication] becomes a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*) when manifested by a word (*pada*), as in:
"He, the perpetrator of fraudulent dice-games, the kindler of the house made of lac, the arrogant one..."
"Where is that Duryodhana—whose servants are the Pāṇḍavas, who are skilled at pulling away the black hair and upper garments [of women];
who is the elder brother of a hundred younger brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana; and who is the friend of the King of Aṅga? Tell us, for we have come here not out of anger, but to see him."

"Will these wretched ones, having fallen into slavery and having us as their sole refuge, do anything? They will surely be humiliated"—these and other thoughts were entertained by you at the time of the gambling match; we have not forgotten them.
A certain remedy for that situation has now been carried out.

By manifesting that meaning through such phrases as "Was nothing accomplished? and so forth, [the speaker] rests solely upon the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) in lines such as "by all those who are masters of the deceptions of gambling.
An example of what is revealed by the sentence (vākyaprakāśya) is as follows:
Hearing the clamor of birds flying up from the bamboo thicket,
the limbs of the young woman, busy with her household chores, grow cold.
"While the young wife, occupied with household chores, hears the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of cane-reeds, her limbs grow weary.
Here, having conveyed the suggested meaning— that a man who had been given a rendezvous has entered the bower of cane creepers— [the verse functions].
The expressed meaning exists by virtue of its own primacy;
and since there is thus no occasion for either direct denotation (*abhidhā*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
suggestion (*dhvanana*) is indeed distinct [from them].
Now, it might be argued: "Whatever word aims at as its ultimate goal is the meaning of that word";
thus, why should even that which is intended as the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) not be the expressed meaning (*vācya*), given that it is the ultimate goal?

In this context, all causal factors (*kāraka*s), by virtue of being causal factors, possess their own operations; therefore, they are being brought to completion [as the object]. Consequently, when there is the utterance of what is already accomplished (*bhūta*) and what is to be accomplished (*bhavya*), [the former serves as the cause for the latter].

"An existent thing is taught for the sake of what is yet to be brought into being"— according to this principle of "burning what is not yet burned," that which has not yet been attended to is what is enjoined;
thus, in some cases, even the meaning of a word denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*) becomes the object [of the injunction],
as in "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "one offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*).

For in this way, even in the case of "the eastern one runs," there would be an intention regarding the western one; [furthermore,] in the theory of the expression of already-connected meanings (*abhihitānvaya*), it is the word-meaning as connected that is expressed,
whereas in the theory of the expression of the connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), it is merely the connected that is expressed.
For it is precisely there that the convention is established;
however, the specific qualified entity (*anvitaviśeṣa*) remains inexpressible according to both philosophical systems.

And if such is the case regarding the expressed meaning (*vācya*), what can be said of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which is by nature the opposite of the expressed? Nor is it possible to say that the suggested meaning is inferable (*anumeya*);
for there is no apprehension of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the expressed and the suggested.
Valid cognition proceeds;
for indeed, that which is to be manifested does not exist without the totality of conditions such as context,
and that [context] is not within the range of valid cognition.
However, there is no fault regarding those [words] that express what is to be indicated (*vyaṅgya*).
For when such a causal totality (*sāmagrī*) has not been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
who can deny the cognition that arises even without depending on logical justification?
Established is *dhvanana* (suggestive function), which is distinct from the operations of direct denotation (*abhidhā*), intentionality (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This has been examined in detail elsewhere; thus it is stated here in brief. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the *Śabdavyāpāravicāra* (An Inquiry into the Function of Words), composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Mammaṭa Ācārya, the sovereign of all learned scholars.
